title: Ten live lanes remain; performance checks depend on the change
meaning: The selected multi-phase planner requires unit verification, exactly ten numbered live lanes, and review of interaction changes. Its performance block accepts Not applicable. with a specific reason and no boxes. Applicable performance verification retains its named boxes and uses a credible concern, existing requirement, or actual platform constraint.
effect: The executable checker enforces the explained performance exemption as well as the remaining live and review gates. A plan can still be rejected for missing mandatory lanes or review evidence. This workflow does not apply automatically to every chat, and it does not impose universal numeric performance caps.
suggestion: Review whether ten live lanes suit the long-running work you select. Keep performance verification tied to the actual change, explain non-applicability, and derive numeric criteria from a relevant requirement, constraint, or agreed target.

title: The benchmark checklist checks measurement quality
meaning: The benchmark checklist checks tuning, errors, whether work really ran, noise, bottlenecks, and end-to-end relevance. A full comparison asks for at least five alternating runs per side.
effect: There is no universal millisecond or throughput limit here. The procedure can still be excessive for a modest question. A requested ballpark already has a one-run exception.
suggestion: Keep honest measurement. Review when the full procedure is justified, and whether lighter evidence can support appropriately qualified claims.

title: Do we always need to explain the bottleneck?
meaning: Explain the Number asks for a decision threshold, noise floor, and a measured limiter before trusting a result.
effect: This protects against false speedup claims. Read literally, it can also prevent a useful qualified observation until a deeper profiling exercise is complete.
suggestion: Distinguish a measured observation from a causal explanation or an adoption recommendation. Decide what evidence each claim needs.

title: Stop optimizing once the chosen target is met
meaning: The performance-fix playbook tries eliminating unused work, reuse, less work, deferral, concurrency, then cheaper work. It stops once an earlier option meets the target.
effect: This is generally an anti-overoptimization rule. The important question is who chose the target; it should not become a silent ceiling on a stronger user request.
suggestion: Keep the ordering as a heuristic, with the target grounded in the user's request or a stated assumption.

locators.contains: When an earlier mantra meets the target

title: Optimization loops can require a minimum number of attempts
meaning: Hillclimb pairs its metric target with an attempt floor. Its example is 50% improvement and ten iterations, not a global setting.
effect: This applies when sustained optimization is selected. It can keep running after an early success; later wording also permits stopping when ideas no longer earn their cost.
suggestion: Make the floor, target, and stopping tradeoff explicit when starting a sustained run. Do not infer this workflow from an ordinary feature request.

title: Statechart has actual exploration and drawing limits
meaning: The tool draws a full graph only up to 500 states. Follow-up checking runs after the first broken rule stop at 100,000 distinct states. The initial check is a different case.
effect: These limit the optional model-checking tool, not the size or performance of software Kishu may build. Unchecked rules must be reported; they do not count as passing.
suggestion: Keep the distinction between drawing and proof visible. If this tool matters to your work, consider configurable limits and a cost decision before bigger runs.

title: Build a tool even for one-off nontrivial work
meaning: Build the Lever defaults to a script, generator, codemod, or delegate skill whenever work is not trivial. It explicitly says repetition is not required.
effect: A rerunnable tool can be valuable proof. Making one compulsory can add maintenance and time when a direct edit plus existing checks would be sufficient.
suggestion: Consider a benefit-based trigger: repeated work, meaningful error risk, or proof that needs to be rerun. Keep the option for one-off work without requiring it.

title: Selecting Architect still means at least two designs
meaning: Kishu removed the rule that crossing a function boundary automatically activates Architect. Inside Architect, two structurally distinct candidates are still required.
effect: The outer trigger is lighter, but the selected workflow can still spend multiple model runs on an otherwise settled design.
suggestion: Decide whether two candidates should be mandatory only when competing approaches are genuinely unresolved or when the user asks for comparison.

title: Smallest change and first-principles redesign can pull apart
meaning: One principle minimizes the diff; another says to redesign around a new requirement as if it were foundational from day one.
effect: Both are useful lenses. An agent can over-refactor if it treats redesign as an instruction to rewrite rather than a way to evaluate the needed change.
suggestion: Clarify that thinking broadly does not authorize broad edits. Expand implementation scope when the requirement or demonstrated defect needs it.

title: The optional comment reviewer has a strong deletion bias
meaning: Comment Sicko keeps only specific exceptions, deletes uncertain comments, and flags internal surprises for code redesign.
effect: Kishu stopped running it before every review. If selected, it can still turn a comment cleanup into pressure for a refactor. Legal headers and public API contracts are explicit exceptions.
suggestion: Consider retaining useful non-obvious rationale and requiring concrete value before restructuring code. Or keep this specialist explicitly opt-in with its current personality.

title: Trust internal types unconditionally
meaning: Boundary Discipline centralizes validation at inputs and treats internal validation as redundant.
effect: This can simplify well-typed pure code. Dynamic inputs, persisted corruption, concurrency, and mixed-language boundaries need more care than a literal unconditional rule permits.
suggestion: Keep boundary validation as the default while allowing checks that protect a real invariant or trust boundary. Avoid adding defensive checks without a concrete failure mode.

title: Some TypeScript rules are stronger than common project conventions
meaning: The skill favors branded primitives, no unchecked casts, object arguments, running real dependencies, and structured logging.
effect: These can improve correctness, but need repository and hot-path context. They are not constraints imposed by TypeScript itself.
suggestion: Review the individual table rows. Preserve useful exceptions and project conventions rather than replacing the entire rule set.

title: Migration and verification principles need compatible boundaries
meaning: Outcome-Oriented Execution allows planned intermediate breakage; Sequence Verifiable Units says not to advance until a unit is green and prescribes trunk-first sequencing.
effect: They can coexist if the verifiable unit is an agreed migration phase. A literal per-edit interpretation can create unnecessary compatibility scaffolding or repeated checks.
suggestion: Define meaningful verification boundaries for the task, preserve useful checks, and leave commit/rebase mechanics to the actual delivery workflow.

title: Fewer polished features must not erase requested capability
meaning: Experience First favors fewer polished features; Subtract Before You Add prefers removal before construction.
effect: These are useful product heuristics. Taken as authority to reduce the brief or clean unrelated code, they conflict with Kishu's scope preservation.
suggestion: Use these principles to discuss tradeoffs, while delivering the agreed capability and asking about material scope changes.

title: Phase and turn budgets should organize work, not shrink the goal
meaning: Guard the Context Window explicitly suggests limiting files per phase, setting turn budgets, and accounting for mechanism costs.
effect: This manages the agent's working context. It is not a stated performance limit on your software or a reason to silently omit requirements.
suggestion: Keep phased execution and compact context. Make any reduction in scope or meaningful quality/cost tradeoff explicit.

title: Kishu already replaces automatic expensive-test skipping
meaning: Test logic that could regress, reuse sufficient coverage, run affected checks, and ask when useful coverage has substantial setup, runtime, service, or maintenance cost.
effect: A declined or unavailable test remains a visible coverage gap. This policy intentionally replaces the upstream cheap-test-only bias.
suggestion: Likely keep. Review the meaning of substantial cost and what an estimate should include, without adding a fixed budget that silently makes the decision for you.

title: Evidence should match the claim and can be reused
meaning: Visual changes get inspected rendered evidence where possible; APIs get actual calls and responses; logic gets executed checks. Evidence is rerun when invalidated, not merely on the next message.
effect: This adds useful proof without making every task produce screenshots, videos, benchmarks, and a report. It does not substitute a screenshot for meaningful tests.
suggestion: Likely keep. Review any workflow that separately reimposes a larger evidence package regardless of the change.

locators.contains: Match the evidence to the work

title: Autonomy must preserve the user's gates and scope
meaning: Kishu restricts side discoveries to necessary authorized work and preserves the expensive-test decision gate. Its router removes automatic security audits, comment deletion, PRs, and unrelated skill repair.
effect: The inherited Never Block on the Human principle is subordinate to these exceptions and host permissions. A reversible action alone is not unlimited authority.
suggestion: Likely keep. Review the exact cases where you want a decision versus an autonomous assumption.

title: Configured model roles do not change the main chat model
meaning: Kishu resolves user/project configuration, checks available models, passes effort separately in Codex, and inherits the parent where appropriate.
effect: Upstream leaf skills still mention their bundled model defaults and cross-family panels. Kishu's router and adapters govern them; an unavailable family must be disclosed, not invented.
suggestion: Keep capability-aware selection. Review any per-role cost policy separately from the software's performance. Your private local model file is not copied into this shareable catalog.

title: PR watching has configurable operational defaults
meaning: The watcher defaults to 60-second polling, 300-second stack sweeps, no timeout, and a five-consecutive-query-error budget.
effect: These control an optional watcher, not the build quality or feature scope. Query-error exhaustion is a tool failure to report, not evidence that a PR passed.
suggestion: Probably keep as visible command options; tune them when a specific monitoring task needs it.

title: Benny's time budgets belong to a separate optional automation
meaning: The bundled Benny example contains triage, reproduction, fixing, follow-up, and artifact-retention budgets.
effect: These are configuration examples for that issue automation. Merely including pstack does not schedule Benny or activate its budgets in every Kishu chat.
suggestion: Leave this out of ordinary-work defaults. Review its settings if you decide to configure the automation.
